kept.excerpt: VCIOM's September 4 release reported party support of 37.2% for United Russia, 11.6% for the Communist Party (CPRF), 11.5% for New People, 8.7% for LDPR and 5.3% for A Just Russia. The survey covered August 24–30, 2026, with 1,600 adult respondents, a combined telephone and household-interview sample, and a stated maximum sampling error of 2.5%.
kept.relevance: This recent primary polling release places LDPR behind both CPRF and New People in voting intention, although it does not project total seats.

kept.excerpt: Vedomosti reported that FOM's August 28–30 survey put United Russia at 33%, LDPR at 11%, CPRF at 9%, New People at 4% and A Just Russia at 3%. LDPR's support increased four percentage points from the preceding survey. FOM interviewed 1,500 respondents in 97 settlements across 51 Russian regions.
kept.relevance: This contemporaneous report supplies a competing poll in which LDPR ranks second in voting intention, documenting substantial disagreement between pollsters before the cutoff.

kept.excerpt: Vedomosti reported that FOM's August 21–23 survey placed CPRF at 10%, LDPR at 7% and New People at 6%, while VCIOM's August 17–23 survey placed them at 11.7%, 9.7% and 10.8%, respectively. Political analyst Ilya Grashchenkov said differences between these parties were within the surveys' statistical margins and that several weeks of sustained movement mattered more than weekly fluctuations. He described CPRF as relying on a disciplined protest electorate, LDPR as trying to preserve Zhirinovsky's legacy, and New People as having growth potential among younger and urban voters.
kept.relevance: This dated expert preview identifies LDPR's principal competitors and explains why close voting-intention readings leave the second-place contest uncertain.

search_notes: Frozen evidence cutoff: 2026-09-07. Included six items with publication dates verified from article metadata or visible publication datelines and article text. Excerpts are factual English translations or condensations of the relevant source passages; expert assessments are explicitly attributed. Searches covered Russian-language polls, the second-place contest, official election scheduling and historical seat results. Excluded publications after the cutoff, including polls published after September 7 even when their fieldwork began earlier, undated rolling polling pages, prediction-market material and all reporting on the 2026 election outcome. Live navigation, related-story links and other later page furniture were excluded from the evidence. web_fetch failed because of a provider-configuration error; article verification used the agent-reach web skill as the requested fallback. No constituency-level seat projection was verified, so polling percentages should not be interpreted as total-seat forecasts.
